blocks.text: Magnetic flux linkage is a key concept in electromagnetism, particularly in the study of inductance and electromagnetic induction. It refers to the product of the magnetic flux through a coil and the number of turns in the coil. It essentially measures how much magnetic flux is linked with the coil due to its multiple turns, and it is an important factor in understanding how coils and inductors operate in electrical circuits.

blocks.title: Magnetic flux linkage
blocks.text: Magnetic flux linkage = Phi = N phi_B ... (10.7), where phi_B is the magnetic flux through a single loop of area A and N is the total number of turns of the coil.

Magnetic flux linkage plays a crucial role in the design and operation of transformers, electric motors, generators and inductors. The concept is particularly important in Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, explored later in this chapter.

When you insert a credit or ATM card into an Automated Teller Machine (ATM), the magnetic strip on the card, which contains millions of tiny magnetic domains held together by a resin binder, is read by the machine; the information encoded on the strip gives you access to your account (For Your Information).

flux through one loop times the number of turns

blocks.prompt: A coil of 10 turns and area 35 cm^2 lies in a perpendicular field of 0.5 T. What is its flux linkage?
blocks.explanation: Flux through one turn: phi_B = BA = 0.5 x 35 x 10^-4 = 1.75 x 10^-3 Wb. Flux linkage = N phi_B = 10 x 1.75 x 10^-3 = 1.75 x 10^-2 Wb. If the coil is pulled out of the field in 1.0 s, this linkage falls to zero and the average induced emf is 1.75 x 10^-2 V (numerical 10.6).

items: Flux linkage = N phi_B (10.7): flux through one loop times the number of turns; central to transformers, motors, generators, inductors and Faraday's law. Card strips store data in tiny magnetic domains.
